title: Homologous parts change shape and size but keep the same relative connexions

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Homologous parts change shape and size but keep the same relative connexions

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Within a class, homologous parts may change to almost any extent in form and size but always remain connected in the same order; for example, the bones of the arm and forearm are never transposed.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the parts may change to almost any extent in form and size, and yet they always remain connected together in the same order.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIII, “Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs”; section “MORPHOLOGY, between members of the same class, between parts of the same individual”. Scope: homologous structures within classes (vertebrate limbs, insect mouthparts, crustacean limbs, flowers)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch13-13: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The invariant-order statement is precise and readily falsifiable. Existing imaging and character data test many examples but do not cover the universal taxonomic scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For homologous serial elements across sampled classes, code topology of anatomical connections and test whether order is invariant despite variation in element size and shape. Any well-supported transposition refutes the universal claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No public dataset exhaustively codes connection order across all cited classes.

Homology assignments can be disputed after fusion or loss.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A no-transposition rule is empirically sharp once parts are homologized independently of their connections. Public anatomy ontologies and specimen repositories cover vertebrate skeletons much better than the full list of organ systems in the claim. Turning those sources into a class-wide connectivity test is months of coding, so only a subset can be resolved with what is already structured.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Represent homologous parts as connectivity graphs and test whether, within a class, adjacency order stays fixed while shape and size vary, using gene expression or developmental identity as the homology criterion. The claim is confirmed if transpositions of connection are absent across tetrapod limbs, arthropod limbs and floral organs, and refuted by well-supported reversals of anatomical order.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Digit identity shifts and homeotic floral changes require an agreed homology standard before they count as transpositions.

Homology has often been defined by conserved connections, so a purely anatomical test can become circular.

Connectivity is coded in an ontology for vertebrate anatomy and is not a downloadable comparative matrix for insect mouthparts, crustacean limbs and flowers together.
